content:
Quick answer: Progress exercise with arthritis by changing one thing at a time, by a small amount, every 1 to 2 weeks. Step up when an exercise feels easy and pain stays acceptable and settles within 24 hours. Hold if you are still adjusting. Step back if pain is worse the next day or a joint swells.

Starting an exercise programme is one challenge; knowing when to do more is another. Do too little and you stop improving. Do too much too soon and you risk a flare that sets you back weeks. The key with arthritis is gradual, planned progression, guided by how your joints respond. This page is a decision guide rather than a calculator: it gives you simple rules and tables to decide each week whether to step up, hold or step back, and shows how to progress each type of exercise.

Why gradual progression matters

Muscles, tendons, bones and joint tissues all adapt to the load you put on them, but they adapt at different speeds. Muscles respond within weeks; tendons and cartilage more slowly. Increasing load gradually gives every tissue time to adjust. NICE guideline NG226 recommends that exercise programmes for osteoarthritis are tailored to the person and reviewed over time, and that people are supported to keep exercising long term. Progressing sensibly is how you keep getting the benefits without setbacks.

The 24-hour pain rule

Many physiotherapists use a simple guide to judge whether exercise is at the right level:

  • During exercise: pain stays at a level you find acceptable, often around 4 out of 10 or lower on a scale where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst imaginable.
  • After exercise: any increase in pain settles back to your usual level within 24 hours.
  • Next morning: stiffness and swelling are no worse than usual.

If all three are true, the level is about right, and you may be ready to progress. If any are not, hold or step back. Some extra muscle aching after new exercise is normal and is not a reason to stop.

The decision table: step up, hold or step back

Use this at the end of each week, or after each session for strength exercises.

What you noticeDecisionWhat to do
Exercise feels easy (effort around 3–4 out of 10), pain acceptable and settles within 24 hours, for 2 sessions or a full weekStep upIncrease one thing by a small amount (see below)
Exercise feels moderately hard (effort 5–7), pain acceptable and settles within 24 hoursHoldStay at this level for another week
Pain higher during exercise, but settles within 24 hoursHold or ease slightlyReduce repetitions, range or speed a little next time
Pain or stiffness worse the next day, or lasting more than 24 hoursStep backReturn to the previous level for a week
Joint swelling, warmth, or a flareStep back moreSwitch to gentle movement until it settles, then restart at about half your previous level
Sharp pain, locking, giving way, or new symptomsStop that exerciseGet advice from a physiotherapist or GP

Rules for any progression

  • Change one thing at a time. For example, add repetitions or add weight, not both at once.
  • Make small changes. A common guide is no more than about 10% more time or distance a week for walking or cycling, and small steps in weight or band strength.
  • Allow time. Stay at each level for at least 1 to 2 weeks before increasing again.
  • Expect ups and downs. Progress is rarely a straight line. A step back is not failure.
  • Plan easier weeks. Every 4 to 6 weeks, an easier week can help you recover and consolidate.

How to progress strength exercises

Work through these steps in order. When you can do the top of one step comfortably for 2 sessions, move to the next.

StepChangeExample: sit-to-stand
1Increase repetitions from 8 towards 128, then 10, then 12 sit-to-stands using hands
2Add a second, then third set2 sets of 12
3Reduce support or increase rangeUse one hand, then no hands; or use a slightly lower chair
4Add resistance, then drop back to 8 repetitionsHold a light weight or a full water bottle, 2 sets of 8
5Slow the movementTake 3 seconds to lower
6Make it more challenging or functionalStep-ups, or sit-to-stand on one leg with support

For band exercises, move up to the next band strength when 12 repetitions feel easy; see our resistance band workouts. For more on choosing weights, see our strength training guide.

How to progress walking

StepChangeExample
1FrequencyWalk 10 minutes, 3 days a week, then 5 days
2DurationAdd 2 to 5 minutes to each walk every week or two
3PaceAdd short brisk spells, such as 1 minute brisk, 2 minutes easy
4TerrainAdd gentle slopes or grass and paths
5StepsAdd 500 to 1,000 steps a day over a week or two

Our guide to walking with arthritis has a full 8-week plan.

How to progress cycling and swimming

  • Cycling: first increase time, then resistance. Keep resistance low enough that you can pedal smoothly without strain on your knees.
  • Swimming and pool exercise: increase session length, then the number of lengths or exercises, then try deeper water or more effort. Change strokes if one aggravates your joints.

How to progress balance and mobility

TypeProgression steps
BalanceTwo hands on support → one hand → fingertips → hands hovering → longer holds → add head turns or a soft surface (with a physio's advice)
MobilityMore repetitions (5 to 10) → larger comfortable range → more sessions a day → seated to standing
StretchingLonger holds (up to 30 seconds) → repeat 2 to 3 times; never force

Worked examples

Example 1: knee osteoarthritis, sit-to-stand

Week 1: 2 sets of 8 using hands, pain 3 out of 10, settles within an hour. Week 2: same, feels easy. Decision: step up to 2 sets of 10. Week 3: pain 4 out of 10, settles overnight. Decision: hold. Week 4: feels easy. Decision: step up to 2 sets of 12.

Example 2: hip osteoarthritis, walking

Walking 20 minutes on 5 days. Increases to 25 minutes. The next morning the hip is stiffer than usual and pain lasts all day. Decision: step back to 20 minutes for a week, then try 22 minutes.

Example 3: rheumatoid arthritis, hand exercises

Doing finger exercises daily, adding putty twice a week. A flare starts, with swollen knuckles. Decision: stop putty, continue gentle range-of-motion only. When the flare settles, restart putty at half the previous amount.

Which thing should you progress first?

If you are unsure what to change, use this order of priority. It suits most people with arthritis:

  1. Consistency first. Before making anything harder, aim to exercise regularly, such as 2 strength sessions and several walks each week, for at least 2 to 3 weeks.
  2. Then amount. Add repetitions, sets or minutes.
  3. Then difficulty. Add resistance, reduce support, increase speed or try a harder variation.
  4. Then variety. Add new exercises or activities that work towards your goals, such as stairs, gardening or a class.

Link your progression to what matters to you. If your goal is to walk to the shops, progress walking time and sit-to-stands. If it is to lift your grandchild, progress squats and carrying.

A 12-week strength progression example

WeeksSets and repetitionsLoad
1–21 set of 8–10Body weight or lightest band
3–42 sets of 10Same
5–62 sets of 12Same
7–82 sets of 8–10Next band or a light weight
9–102–3 sets of 10–12Same
11–12Easier week, then reviewChoose the next step with the decision table

This is a typical pattern only. Use the decision table each week; some people move faster, others need to repeat weeks.

Adjusting for different types of arthritis

ConditionProgression tips
OsteoarthritisSteady progression works well; expect some ache that settles. Load is generally good for joints when increased gradually
Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritisProgress during settled periods; scale back quickly during flares. Fatigue may limit you more than pain, so watch energy levels too
Axial spondyloarthritisDaily mobility plus progressive strength and fitness; regular exercise is an important part of treatment
GoutProgress between attacks; avoid exercising an acutely inflamed joint
Fibromyalgia alongside arthritisVery small steps and pacing are important; increase more slowly than the general guide

For what to do when a flare interrupts your plan, see our guide to exercise during a flare-up.

Common progression mistakes

  • Doing too much on a good day. Stick to the plan even when you feel great; boom-and-bust patterns often lead to flares.
  • Changing several things at once. If you add weight, sets and a new exercise together and your knee flares, you will not know why.
  • Never progressing. Doing the same easy routine for months maintains, but rarely improves, strength and fitness.
  • Ignoring the next day. How you feel the morning after is often the most useful signal.
  • Restarting at full level after a break. Step back first, then build up.

A weekly check-in template

Copy this into a notebook or your phone and fill it in at the end of each week.

QuestionYour answer
What did I do this week (sessions, minutes, sets, repetitions, weights)?
How hard did it feel (0 to 10)?
Highest pain during exercise (0 to 10)?
Did pain settle within 24 hours?Yes / No
Any swelling, warmth or flare?Yes / No
Decision for next weekStep up / Hold / Step back
The one thing I will change

If detailed logging feels like a chore, our guide to tracking progress without constant measuring suggests simpler ways.

After a flare or a break

If you have had to stop for a flare, illness or holiday, do not restart where you left off. A useful guide is to restart at about half your previous level after a break of 1 to 2 weeks, and lower after longer breaks, then build back up over 2 to 4 weeks using the decision table. You will usually regain fitness faster than it took to build initially.

Signs you are progressing well

  • Everyday tasks such as stairs, getting out of a chair or carrying shopping feel easier.
  • You can walk further or for longer.
  • Your usual pain is the same or lower.
  • You feel more confident and have more energy.

Strength improvements are often noticeable within 6 to 8 weeks, with further gains over months.

When to see a GP or physiotherapist

  • You keep having to step back and cannot get past a certain level.
  • Pain is steadily worsening over weeks despite reducing exercise.
  • A joint locks, gives way, or swells repeatedly.
  • You are not sure how to progress after joint surgery.
  • You notice new symptoms such as numbness, tingling or weakness.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever. Call 999 for chest pain or severe breathlessness during exercise.

How quickly should I increase exercise with arthritis?

Increase one thing at a time, by a small amount, every 1 to 2 weeks, as long as pain stays acceptable and settles within 24 hours. For walking or cycling, a common guide is no more than about 10% more a week.

Is it normal for joints to ache after exercise?

Some extra ache that settles within 24 hours is normal, especially when starting or progressing. Pain that lasts longer or comes with swelling suggests you should step back.

When should I increase the weight?

When you can do 2 or 3 sets of 12 repetitions with good form and the exercise feels easy, increase the weight slightly and drop back to 8 repetitions.

Should I progress if I have pain?

You can progress with mild pain if it stays at an acceptable level and settles within 24 hours. If pain is higher the next day, hold or step back.

Is there an exercise progression calculator?

We have not built a calculator because the right progression depends on how your joints respond, not a formula. The decision table on this page lets you make that judgement each week. A physiotherapist can personalise it further.

How long until I see progress?

Many people notice easier everyday tasks within a few weeks, with clearer strength gains after 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise.
